topic: Hanging dial spring scale: how a scale turns weight into a needle reading. The load pulls a crossbar down and stretches two springs (Hooke's law: twice the weight, twice the stretch); a rack on the crossbar turns a small pinion gear that carries the needle.
title: How a Scale Knows the Weight ⚖️
principle: In a dial spring balance the load pulls a crossbar down against springs whose stretch is proportional to the load (Hooke's law); a rack fixed to the crossbar meshes with a pinion on the pointer shaft, so the pointer turns in proportion to the stretch and the dial marks are evenly spaced.

How a Scale Knows the Weight ⚖️
Guess: what turns the needle? 👇

firstComment:
Answer: a tiny gear 🔧

Inside a dial spring scale, the load pulls a crossbar down, and the crossbar stretches two springs. A spring stretches in proportion to the pull (Hooke's law): twice the weight, twice the stretch.

A toothed bar called a rack is fixed to the crossbar. As it slides down, its teeth turn a small gear (the pinion), and the needle sits on the pinion's shaft. So the needle turns in proportion to the stretch, and that's why the marks on the dial are evenly spaced.

The springs do the weighing. The gear only reads how far they stretched.

(Simplified 3D model of a hanging dial scale, with example numbers. Real scales also have a small spring that keeps the rack pressed on the gear, and bathroom scales add levers.)

Sources:
Britannica, Spring balance (if the load is doubled, the deformation is doubled; the springs' upper ends are attached to the casing and the lower ends to a crossbar; the pinion carrying the pointer meshes with the rack on the crossbar, so stretching the springs rotates the pointer): https://www.britannica.com/technology/spring-balance
Wikipedia, Weighing scale (the heavier the object, the more the spring stretches, as described in Hooke's law; rack and pinion mechanisms are often used to convert the linear spring motion to a dial reading): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighing_scale
TryEngineering (IEEE), Spring Scale Engineering (the extension of a spring is in direct proportion to the weight added, so the markings on a spring scale are equally spaced): https://tryengineering.org/resource/lesson-plan/spring-scale-engineering/
HowStuffWorks, Inside a Bathroom Scale (levers pass the weight to a spring; a rack and pinion turns the dial): https://home.howstuffworks.com/inside-scale.htm

Under the question How does it weigh this? a red circle marks the center of the dial; a 2 kg steel weight drops into the pan and the needle swings to 2. The middle of the dial fades away to show the inside: two coil springs hang from a bracket and hold a crossbar; a brass toothed rack stands on the crossbar and meshes with a small brass gear on the needle's shaft. 1, weight stretches the springs: a 2 kg weight is set in the pan, the crossbar moves down and the springs get longer. 2, the rack turns the gear: a second 2 kg weight is set on the first, then up close the rack slides down, its teeth turn the gear and the needle moves from 2 to 4 kg. 3, 2x weight = 2x stretch: two equal brackets show that each 2 kg stretches the springs by the same amount, and two equal arcs on the dial show the evenly spaced marks. The payoff reads Springs feel the weight, the gear reads it. The dial closes, the weights are lifted off, a follow line appears and the video loops.
